name: Dental sandpaper strips

lead: Dental sandpaper strips are gritty strips sold online to scrape surface stain from teeth, for a lighter look. They are distinct from peroxide whitening strips, which use a chemical bleaching agent.

They remove stain by mechanical abrasion and cannot change the intrinsic colour of the tooth. Dentists remove extrinsic stain by scaling and polishing with abrasive pastes, an in-office procedure that removes roughly one micron of enamel per treatment. No studies of consumer abrasive strips were found.

paras: Users rub a strip across the front surfaces of the teeth for a short time, as an occasional stain-removal step. Others get a professional scale and polish instead, which uses abrasive pastes under a dentist's control.
Dental literature lists abrasion as a cause of tooth wear, and enamel does not regrow. The abrasivity of these strips is not standardised.

angle.text: Online marketplaces sell abrasive strips for scraping surface stain off teeth, distinct from peroxide strips. They work by rubbing stain away, the same principle as a professional polish but without controlled abrasivity. No studies or standard abrasivity data exist for them.

lead: Dental sandpaper strips are abrasive strips sold online, mainly through marketplaces, that are marketed for scraping stains off teeth. They are distinct from peroxide whitening strips, which use a chemical bleaching agent.[1]

Dentists remove extrinsic stain by scaling and polishing with abrasive pastes, an in-office procedure that removes roughly one micron of enamel per treatment.[1][2] Whitening products sold to consumers are usually peroxide-based or abrasive toothpastes.[1]
No studies of consumer abrasive strips were found.

paras: The strips carry an abrasive grit similar in concept to fine sandpaper and are promoted for rubbing off coffee, tea or tobacco stain. Extrinsic stains from coffee, tea, red wine and tobacco sit on the tooth surface and are generally removable by cleaning.[1][3]

Professional prophylaxis polishes with abrasive paste; selective polishing is now recommended by many educational institutions over routine full-mouth polishing, since polishing is largely cosmetic.[2] Whitening toothpastes contain more abrasives and detergents than regular ones, and excessive use may damage enamel.[4][1] Toothpastes with RDA above 250 could damage tooth surfaces.[4]

Abrasion is defined as tooth loss from physical means other than tooth contact, and high-abrasivity toothpaste is listed among its contributing factors.[5] Enamel is not regenerated by the body.[6] The grit and abrasivity of consumer strips is not standardised in the sources reviewed.
